label: Inference Parameters, RAG & Agents — Part A

questions.scenario: A content marketing team uses Amazon Bedrock to draft blog posts. They notice that outputs always follow identical patterns with predictable word choices. The team wants more variety while keeping responses on-topic.
questions.stem: Which parameter adjustment achieves this goal?

options.text: Decrease the response length to force concise answers
Increase the temperature to broaden the probability distribution over candidate tokens
Add stop sequences to end generation at paragraph boundaries
Switch to a different foundation model in a separate AWS Region

explanation.correct: Temperature controls randomness in token selection. Higher temperature flattens the probability distribution, making less probable tokens more likely to be chosen — producing more varied and creative outputs while keeping the model on the same topic.

distractors.A: Response length limits output size but does not affect variety in word choice or sentence structure.
distractors.C: Stop sequences control where generation ends, not how diverse the content is within that generation.
distractors.D: AWS Region affects latency and data residency. It does not change model generation behavior.

questions.scenario: A developer sets temperature=0.9, Top K=250, and Top P=0.95 for a medical symptom checker in Amazon Bedrock. The application sometimes generates plausible-sounding but clinically incorrect recommendations.
questions.stem: Which parameter change would MOST reduce the risk of generating incorrect medical information?

options.text: Increase Top K to 500 to consider more token candidates
Increase temperature to 1.0 to explore the full token space
Lower temperature closer to 0 to make outputs more deterministic and favor highest-probability tokens
Remove all stop sequences to allow longer, more detailed responses

explanation.correct: Lower temperature concentrates probability on the most likely tokens, producing more predictable, consistent outputs. For factual applications like medical advice, deterministic responses reduce the risk of sampling low-probability (potentially incorrect) completions.

distractors.A: Increasing Top K expands the candidate pool, which increases diversity and randomness — the opposite of what's needed for factual accuracy.
distractors.B: Higher temperature increases randomness, making it more likely to generate creative but potentially incorrect content.
distractors.D: Response length does not affect factual accuracy. Longer responses can still contain incorrect information.

questions.scenario: A pharmaceutical company's foundation model confidently states that a drug approved 3 months ago has no known interactions with statins. The model was trained 18 months ago, and the drug's interaction profile was only published last quarter.
questions.stem: Which technique addresses this type of knowledge gap without retraining?

options.text: Increase Top P to sample from a wider token distribution
Fine-tune the model on the new drug interaction data
Implement RAG to retrieve current drug interaction data from an external knowledge base at inference time
Deploy a larger version of the same foundation model

explanation.correct: RAG retrieves information from external data sources at inference time, allowing the model to access knowledge published after its training cutoff. The drug interaction database can be kept current without retraining the model.

distractors.A: Top P controls generation diversity, not knowledge. Wider sampling cannot introduce information the model never learned.
distractors.B: Fine-tuning would work but requires retraining. RAG provides current knowledge without model modification, which is faster and cheaper for frequently updated data.
distractors.D: A larger model trained at the same time has the same knowledge cutoff. Size does not add post-training information.

questions.scenario: An e-commerce company processes 50,000 product descriptions through an embedding model and stores the resulting vectors. A customer searches 'comfortable shoes for standing all day' and receives results including orthopedic insoles and anti-fatigue mats — items never containing the word 'shoes'.
questions.stem: What explains how these semantically related but keyword-different results were retrieved?

options.text: The vector database performed keyword expansion by adding synonyms to the search query
The embedding model memorized associations between product categories during training
The database returned random results because the exact search terms were not found
Vector embeddings capture semantic meaning, so items addressing foot comfort and standing fatigue have similar vector representations regardless of exact wording

explanation.correct: Vector embeddings are numerical representations of meaning and relationships. Products addressing similar concepts (foot comfort, standing fatigue) have nearby vectors in embedding space, enabling retrieval based on semantic similarity rather than keyword overlap.

distractors.A: Vector search operates on mathematical similarity between embeddings, not keyword expansion or synonym matching.
distractors.B: Embeddings capture general semantic relationships from training, not memorized product-category associations. They generalize to unseen combinations.
distractors.C: Vector databases always return nearest neighbors by similarity. They never return random results — even dissimilar content gets a relevance score.

questions.scenario: A customer asks an AI travel assistant: 'Book me the cheapest flight from Nairobi to London next Friday, then reserve a hotel near Heathrow for two nights.' The system must check flight APIs, compare prices, execute a booking, then search hotel availability and confirm a reservation.
questions.stem: Why can't a foundation model alone fulfill this request?

options.text: Foundation models cannot understand multi-step requests in natural language
Foundation models can only process requests in English, not multi-city routing
Foundation models lack the context window to process requests longer than one sentence
Foundation models generate text but cannot execute actions against external systems — agents are needed to orchestrate API calls and complete real-world tasks

explanation.correct: Foundation models understand and generate language but cannot complete real-world tasks requiring interaction with external systems. Agents orchestrate between the FM, APIs, and knowledge bases to break down tasks and execute actions.

distractors.A: Foundation models understand complex multi-step requests well. The limitation is executing actions, not understanding intent.
distractors.B: Foundation models handle multilingual and multi-entity requests. The limitation is action execution, not language understanding.
distractors.C: Modern foundation models have large context windows handling thousands of tokens. Request length is not the constraint here.

questions.scenario: A developer is configuring Amazon Bedrock inference parameters for a customer service chatbot that must provide consistent, factual answers about company policies.
questions.stem: Which parameter configurations would make responses MORE deterministic and consistent? (Select TWO)

options.text: Set temperature close to 0 to concentrate probability on the most likely tokens
Set Top K to a low value to restrict the candidate token pool
Set temperature to 1.0 to explore the full probability distribution
Set Top P to 0.99 to include nearly all tokens as candidates
Remove all stop sequences to allow maximum response generation

explanation.correct: Low temperature concentrates selection on highest-probability tokens (more deterministic), and low Top K restricts the candidate pool to fewer top tokens. Both reduce randomness and increase response consistency.

distractors.C: Temperature 1.0 uses the full probability distribution without dampening, maximizing diversity rather than consistency.
distractors.D: Top P at 0.99 includes nearly all tokens as candidates, which increases diversity rather than restricting it.
distractors.E: Stop sequences control response termination, not randomness or consistency of content.

questions.stem: Which AWS services support vector storage for embedding-based retrieval in AI applications? (Select THREE)

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Service
Amazon Aurora with vector extensions
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector
Amazon CloudFront
AWS Step Functions
Amazon EventBridge

explanation.correct: OpenSearch Service provides native vector search capabilities. Aurora supports vector extensions for similarity search. RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector enables vector storage and similarity queries within a relational database.

distractors.D: CloudFront is a content delivery network for caching static assets. It does not store or query vector embeddings.
distractors.E: Step Functions orchestrates workflows. It does not provide data storage or vector search capabilities.
distractors.F: EventBridge routes events between services. It is not a storage or search engine for vector data.

questions.scenario: An architect is designing a RAG pipeline for a financial advisory chatbot. They need to understand the complete data flow from document ingestion to user response.
questions.stem: Which steps occur during the retrieval phase of a RAG query? (Select THREE)

options.text: The user query is converted into a vector embedding using the same embedding model that processed the source documents
The query embedding is compared against stored document embeddings using similarity search
Retrieved passages are combined with the original query as context for the LLM to generate a response
The foundation model's weights are updated with the retrieved information
The vector database generates the final user-facing response directly
All documents in the knowledge base are sent to the LLM regardless of relevance

explanation.correct: RAG flow: (1) query is embedded using the same model as source documents, (2) the embedding searches the vector DB by similarity, (3) retrieved passages augment the prompt sent to the LLM for generation.

distractors.D: RAG operates at inference time without modifying model weights. The model remains unchanged throughout the process.
distractors.E: Vector databases retrieve relevant passages. The LLM generates the final response using retrieved context.
distractors.F: Only semantically relevant passages are retrieved. Sending all documents would exceed context limits and reduce response quality.

questions.stem: What capabilities distinguish Agents for Amazon Bedrock from a standalone foundation model invocation? (Select THREE)

options.text: Automatic task decomposition — breaking complex requests into orchestrated sub-steps
API action execution — calling external services to complete real-world tasks
Knowledge base invocation — retrieving contextual information to inform decisions
Model pre-training — training new foundation models from scratch
Weight modification — updating the FM's parameters after each interaction
Hardware provisioning — automatically scaling GPU instances

explanation.correct: Agents automatically decompose tasks into steps (orchestration), execute API calls against external systems (actions), and invoke knowledge bases for contextual information — capabilities a standalone FM call cannot perform.

distractors.D: Agents orchestrate existing models. Pre-training is a separate, resource-intensive process unrelated to agent functionality.
distractors.E: Agents do not modify model weights. They use the FM as-is while orchestrating external interactions.
distractors.F: Infrastructure scaling is handled by AWS compute services. Agents orchestrate logic, not hardware.

questions.stem: Which problems does RAG solve compared to relying solely on a foundation model's training data? (Select TWO)

options.text: Provides access to information published after the model's training cutoff date
Reduces hallucination by grounding responses in retrieved factual content
Eliminates the need for any foundation model in the response pipeline
Automatically corrects all mathematical reasoning errors in model outputs
Removes the need for inference parameter configuration

explanation.correct: RAG overcomes knowledge cutoff limitations by retrieving current information at inference time. It also reduces hallucination by providing factual context that grounds the model's generation in verified data.

distractors.C: RAG augments a foundation model — it requires an LLM to generate responses from retrieved context. It does not replace the model.
distractors.D: RAG provides factual grounding but does not fix reasoning capabilities. Mathematical errors stem from model logic, not missing data.
distractors.E: Inference parameters still control generation behavior (temperature, length) when using RAG. They serve different purposes.

questions.scenario: A law firm implements RAG connecting their FM to a knowledge base of 50,000 case law documents. An attorney queries about a 2024 ruling, but the system returns a response mixing accurate retrieved facts with fabricated case citations that don't exist.
questions.stem: What does this behavior indicate about RAG's limitations?

options.text: The vector database corrupted the stored embeddings during retrieval
RAG eliminates all hallucination, so the system must have a configuration error
RAG reduces but does not eliminate hallucination — the LLM can still generate fabricated content alongside retrieved facts
The embedding model used for indexing is incompatible with the retrieval model

explanation.correct: RAG reduces hallucination by providing factual grounding but does not eliminate it. The LLM may still generate plausible-sounding content beyond what was retrieved, especially when retrieved passages partially address the query.

distractors.A: Vector databases reliably store and return embeddings. Corruption would cause retrieval failures, not mixed accurate/fabricated content.
distractors.B: RAG is not a guarantee against hallucination. It improves factual grounding but the generative model can still produce fabricated content.
distractors.D: Embedding incompatibility would cause poor retrieval relevance, not fabricated citations mixed with accurate content.

questions.scenario: An enterprise has internal documents spread across 15 S3 buckets, multiple Confluence wikis, and several SharePoint sites. They want a single RAG interface where their FM can retrieve from all these sources without custom pipeline code.
questions.stem: Which AWS capability provides this fully managed multi-source RAG integration?

options.text: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store with scheduled ingestion jobs
Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock with configured data source connectors
AWS Glue crawlers indexing all sources into a unified catalog
Amazon Kendra enterprise search with FAQ documents

explanation.correct: Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock provides fully managed RAG, connecting foundation models to company data across multiple sources. It handles embedding generation, vector storage, and retrieval without custom pipeline code.

distractors.A: Feature Store manages ML training features, not RAG retrieval. It does not connect FMs to document knowledge bases.
distractors.C: Glue crawlers catalog data schemas for ETL. They do not provide embedding-based retrieval or FM integration.
distractors.D: Kendra provides enterprise search but is a different service from Knowledge Bases for Bedrock. The question specifies RAG with an FM, which is Bedrock's capability.

questions.scenario: A developer tests the same prompt 10 times with temperature=0.0 and gets identical responses each time. They then set temperature=0.8 and get 10 different variations.
questions.stem: What mechanism explains this behavior difference?

options.text: Temperature=0 routes requests to a cached response store instead of the model
At temperature=0 the model always selects the single highest-probability token; at higher temperatures it samples probabilistically from multiple candidates
Temperature=0 uses a smaller version of the model that has fewer possible outputs
Temperature=0.8 causes the model to randomly generate tokens without considering the prompt

explanation.correct: Temperature scales the logits before softmax. At 0 (or near 0), the highest-probability token is always selected (greedy decoding). At higher values, the distribution flattens, allowing probabilistic sampling from multiple candidates.

distractors.A: There is no cached response store. The model still processes the full forward pass — it just deterministically selects the top token each time.
distractors.C: The same model processes both requests. Temperature affects the sampling strategy over the model's output distribution, not the model itself.
distractors.D: At temperature=0.8, the model still conditions on the prompt. It samples from a broader distribution over relevant tokens, not randomly.

questions.stem: A RAG system uses embedding model A to index 100,000 documents into a vector database. At query time, the system uses embedding model B (a different architecture) to encode user queries before searching the vector database.

options.text: Results will be poor because different embedding models produce incompatible vector spaces — the same concept maps to different regions in each model's space
Results will be accurate because vector databases normalize all embeddings to a common format
Results will be faster because using two models distributes the computational load
Results will be identical to using a single model because all embeddings encode the same language

explanation.correct: Each embedding model learns its own vector space. 'Comfortable shoes' might map to region X in model A but region Y in model B. Similarity search requires queries and documents to share the same embedding space.

distractors.B: Vector databases store and search vectors as-is. They do not normalize or translate between different models' embedding spaces.
distractors.C: Using mismatched models doesn't improve speed — it produces semantically meaningless similarity scores because the vector spaces are incompatible.
distractors.D: Different models encode language differently. The vector spaces are not interchangeable even though both process the same language.

questions.scenario: A retail company's Bedrock Agent receives the request: 'Check if the blue sneakers in size 10 are in stock, and if so, add them to my cart and apply my loyalty discount.' The agent must interact with inventory, cart, and loyalty APIs.
questions.stem: How does the agent determine the sequence of API calls?

options.text: A developer must pre-program every possible action sequence in the agent configuration
The agent randomly calls APIs until it achieves the desired outcome
The agent uses the foundation model to decompose the request into logical steps and generates orchestration logic dynamically
The agent sends the entire request to all APIs simultaneously and merges the responses

explanation.correct: Agents for Amazon Bedrock automatically break down tasks and generate orchestration logic using the foundation model. The FM reasons about the task, identifies dependencies (check stock before adding to cart), and determines the correct API sequence.

distractors.A: Agents dynamically generate orchestration logic rather than requiring pre-programmed sequences for every possible request combination.
distractors.B: Agents reason about task structure and dependencies. They plan logical sequences, not trial-and-error random calls.
distractors.D: Agents respect task dependencies (must check stock before adding to cart). They orchestrate sequential and conditional calls based on prior results.

questions.scenario: A company's RAG system retrieves product documentation to answer customer questions. They notice that when users ask vague questions, the retriever returns irrelevant passages and the FM generates unhelpful responses.
questions.stem: Which approaches can improve retrieval quality in this RAG pipeline? (Select TWO)

options.text: Chunk source documents into smaller, more focused segments before embedding to improve retrieval precision
Use query expansion or rephrasing to generate more specific search embeddings from vague user input
Increase the FM's temperature to generate more creative responses from irrelevant passages
Remove the retrieval step and rely solely on the FM's training knowledge
Store raw text without embeddings and use keyword search instead

explanation.correct: Smaller, focused document chunks produce more precise embeddings (reducing noise from long passages). Query expansion or rephrasing converts vague inputs into more specific search vectors that better match relevant content.

distractors.C: Higher temperature adds randomness to generation but cannot make irrelevant passages become relevant. The retrieval problem must be solved upstream.
distractors.D: Removing retrieval eliminates the knowledge advantage of RAG. The FM's training data may lack the specific product information needed.
distractors.E: Keyword search loses semantic understanding. Vector embeddings capture meaning, which is essential for handling varied user phrasings.

questions.stem: Beyond storing embeddings, what operational capabilities do purpose-built vector databases provide? (Select TWO)

options.text: Efficient approximate nearest-neighbor search optimized for high-dimensional vectors
Data management features including fault tolerance, authentication, and access control
Automatic generation of embeddings from raw text without an embedding model
Foundation model training and fine-tuning capabilities
Natural language response generation from stored vectors

explanation.correct: Vector databases provide optimized similarity search algorithms (ANN indices like HNSW) for fast lookup in high-dimensional spaces, plus enterprise features like fault tolerance, authentication, access control, and data management.

distractors.C: Embedding generation requires a separate embedding model. Vector databases store and search pre-computed embeddings, not generate them.
distractors.D: Model training is handled by ML platforms (SageMaker, Bedrock). Vector databases provide storage and retrieval services.
distractors.E: Response generation requires an LLM. Vector databases return stored data and similarity scores, not generated text.

questions.scenario: A banking agent built with Amazon Bedrock handles customer requests like 'Transfer $500 from checking to savings, then show me this month's spending by category.' The agent must interact with multiple backend services.
questions.stem: Which components does the agent orchestrate to fulfill this multi-step financial request? (Select THREE)

options.text: The foundation model — to understand the request and plan the execution steps
External APIs — to execute the transfer and retrieve transaction data
Knowledge bases — to look up account policies or category definitions
Model pre-training pipeline — to retrain the FM on the customer's financial history
SageMaker training jobs — to build a custom model for this customer
CloudFormation — to provision new infrastructure for each request

explanation.correct: Agents orchestrate: the FM (understanding and planning), external APIs (executing actions like transfers and data retrieval), and knowledge bases (supplementing with policy information). This orchestration enables real-world task completion.

distractors.D: Agents do not retrain models. They use the existing FM's capabilities to reason about tasks and plan actions.
distractors.E: Per-customer models are not built at request time. Agents use existing models and external data to personalize responses.
distractors.F: Infrastructure is pre-provisioned. Agents make API calls to existing services, not deploy new infrastructure per request.

questions.scenario: A news organization wants users to search their archive of 5 million articles by describing what they remember about a story ('that article about the tech CEO who sailed across the Atlantic') rather than requiring exact headlines or dates.
questions.stem: How does Amazon OpenSearch Service enable this type of search?

options.text: Full-text inverted index matching keywords in the search query against article content
SQL queries against structured metadata tables storing article attributes
Vector search using language-based embeddings that match semantic meaning rather than exact keywords
Regular expression pattern matching against article titles

explanation.correct: OpenSearch's vector database capabilities use language-based embeddings to match semantic meaning. A description of a story concept matches articles about that topic regardless of whether the exact words appear in the article.

distractors.A: Inverted index keyword search would miss articles that discuss the same topic using different terminology. Semantic search handles this.
distractors.B: SQL against metadata would require structured fields. The user's description doesn't map to structured attributes like date or author.
distractors.D: Regex matches character patterns, not meaning. It cannot connect 'tech CEO who sailed' to an article using different phrasing.

questions.scenario: A developer configures Top P=0.1 for a code completion model. The model generates syntactically correct but extremely predictable completions, always choosing the most common patterns even when the context suggests a less common but more appropriate approach.
questions.stem: What is happening with this Top P configuration?

options.text: Top P=0.1 means the model only considers 10 tokens total regardless of their probability
Top P=0.1 forces the model to skip the top 10% of tokens and sample from less likely ones
Top P=0.1 reduces the model's context window to 10% of its maximum capacity

Top P=0.1 restricts sampling to tokens covering only 10% of cumulative probability, limiting the model to the most probable tokens and preventing exploration of less common but contextually appropriate completions

explanation.correct: Top P (nucleus sampling) includes tokens from the probability distribution until cumulative probability reaches the threshold. At 0.1, only tokens comprising the top 10% of probability mass are considered — heavily restricting variety to the most predictable completions.

distractors.A: Top P is probability-based, not count-based. That description matches Top K (which limits by count). Top P limits by cumulative probability mass.
distractors.B: Top P includes the top tokens up to the threshold, not skips them. It restricts sampling TO the most probable tokens.
distractors.C: Top P controls token sampling during generation. It has no effect on the model's context window or input capacity.
